title: Salvation came to this house (Luke 19:1–10)
hook: Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and repays four times over

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartimaeus shouted louder, and Jesus stood still and asked, what do you want? Who did you stop for? Day five hundred sixty-eight.

Still in Jericho. The first half of this story is the part with the tree: a short, rich chief tax collector named Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore tree to see over the crowd, and Jesus stops underneath and calls him by name. "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Today we follow them inside. Because what Zacchaeus says at his own table, with the whole town grumbling outside, is a speech nobody asked him for. Luke records no sermon from Jesus first. Zacchaeus just stands up.
screen: `TODAY I MUST ABIDE AT THY HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First the grumbling. Luke says they all murmured, "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." Luke has already told us Zacchaeus is a chief among the tax collectors, and rich; to the crowd, that made him a sinner. Then Zacchaeus stands and says, in the King James Bible: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Half to the poor. And fourfold back to anyone he cheated. Here's why fourfold is striking. The law of Moses had rules for paying back what you'd taken. For many wrongs, you returned it and added a fifth. But for a stolen sheep, Exodus says: "he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep." Zacchaeus reaches past the added fifth to the sheep thief's penalty, as if he'd stolen sheep from every one of them. And nobody told him to. Jesus never mentioned money. Being welcomed did what lectures hadn't. A few scholars point out that the Greek verbs are present tense, I give, I restore, and wonder if he's describing what he already does. Others read it as a new promise, there and then. Then Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham." This day. Luke comes back to that word at big moments. The angels used it at his birth: born this day. Jesus used it in Nazareth: this day, this scripture is fulfilled. And on the cross, he'll say today again. Salvation in Luke isn't only someday. It walks into a house, sits down to dinner, and changes how the money moves.
screen: then, large: `THIS DAY IS SALVATION COME TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repay someone generously. Settle and breathe. Think back. Is there anyone you owe something to? Money you borrowed and forgot, a favor never returned, credit you took that was really theirs, time you took from someone without giving back. Don't spiral into guilt. Just pick one. Now imagine paying it back, not exactly, but generously, more than you owe, the way Zacchaeus did. What would that look like? A check, a thank-you, a public word giving them the credit. If you pray, you can give thanks for being welcomed first. The bell holds the time.
Zacchaeus. The rich, short chief tax collector who climbed a tree to see Jesus, then gave half his goods to the poor and repaid everyone he'd cheated fourfold.
Your line: today, salvation. Today, pay back the one thing you thought of, and add a little extra. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: The story of Zacchaeus is read when Christians talk about repentance that changes behavior; Catholic and Orthodox teaching count making restitution as part of turning back after a wrong, and in the Roman Rite the story is read at the dedication of a church.

original.note: Greek: today, this day. a word Luke returns to, from the angels' song to the cross.

trapdoor: what you thought: a short man climbs a tree.
what it means: welcomed before he changed, Zacchaeus changes how his money moves, and salvation arrives today, in his house.
what a scholar hears: fourfold is the Exodus penalty for a stolen sheep, the present-tense verbs are debated, and today threads through Luke from the birth to the cross.

notes: Year one (day 59, 'he knows your name') told the tree-climbing; this day centers the restitution and 'today'.
Restitution laws: add a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7); fourfold for a sheep (Exodus 22:1). Confirm.
Present-tense debate (δίδωμι, ἀποδίδωμι in 19:8): minority 'customary' reading presented as 'a few scholars'. Confirm.
Luke 2:11 and 4:21 are alluded to without quotation ('born this day', 'this day, this scripture is fulfilled').
Dedication-of-a-church reading (Luke 19:1–10): traditional in the Roman Rite. Confirm.

Editor review (y2 557–574 pass): fixed a factual slip: fourfold is not "the steepest standard" (Exodus 22:1 sets fivefold for an ox); it now says he reaches past the added fifth to the sheep thief's penalty. Also cut the superlative "one of the most surprising speeches in the Gospels", "you probably know", the uncited claim that tax collectors "often took more than they were owed", "most read it as a new promise", and "today is one of Luke's favorite words" (teach, screen, myth and original note); howItsDone softened.
